name: Bilberry extract

card.summary: Anthocyanin-rich European blueberry extract with a folk reputation for vision; trials are small and no cosmetic eye-brightening evidence exists.
card.aka: Vaccinium myrtillus, European blueberry, whortleberry, blaeberry
card.note: Reputation for eyes rests on folklore and anecdote; no published trial tests it for brightening eyes.

quick.overview:
Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) is a dark-berried shrub of northern Europe, related to the blueberry. Its fruit and standardised extracts are sold as supplements, traditionally for eye complaints.

In appearance circles it is sometimes mentioned for brighter eyes. Registered trials of bilberry cover dry eye, blood sugar, lipids, cognition and heart disease, and none listed targets cosmetic eye appearance.
quick.mechanism: The berries are rich in anthocyanins, pigments with antioxidant properties in laboratory studies. Proposed mechanisms for eye or vascular effects are largely extrapolated from lab and animal work.
quick.risks: Whole berries are a common food. Encyclopedic sources report no proven health benefit from eating them and note that a review of low-quality studies found no evidence of improved night vision. Supplement quality and interactions are not covered by the sources reviewed.

lead: Bilberry (Vaccinium myrtillus) is a low-growing shrub native to northern Europe, with dark blue-black berries that are eaten fresh and processed into jams, liqueurs and dried powders or standardised extracts sold as dietary supplements [1][2]. The berries are rich in anthocyanins, along with other polyphenols and tannins [2].

Bilberry has a folk reputation for helping the eyes. A frequently repeated anecdote describes British pilots in World War II attributing better night vision to bilberry jam; this story is reported in a secondary source as an anecdote [1]. Encyclopedic sources state that there is no proof that eating bilberries gives health benefits, and that one review of low-quality clinical studies found no evidence that they improve night vision [2].

In looksmaxxing contexts, bilberry extract appears under claims that it can make eyes look brighter. No clinical trial in the sources reviewed tests that claim; registered studies concern dry eye, glycaemic response, lipids, cognition and cardiovascular recovery [3][4].

paras: Bilberry is a perennial shrub of heaths and coniferous forests across northern Europe, with some range in northern Asia and North America. It is distinct from, though related to, cultivated blueberries and cranberries [1]. Regional names include whortleberry, blaeberry and European blueberry [1].
Reported anthocyanin content is high, and laboratory analyses of berries describe anthocyanins as the main phenolic constituents of bilberry [1][5].

A registered trial of bilberry-containing capsules for dry eye enrolled 80 participants [3]. Other registered studies examine bilberry for myocardial infarction recovery (a phase 4 trial, n=50, and a larger trial of bilberry and oat intake, n=900) [4][6], glycaemic response (small studies, n=8 and n=32) [7][8], blood lipids with black rice anthocyanins (n=55) [9], metabolism in healthy people (n=80) [10] and cognition and mood (n=61 and n=76) [11][12]. The registry entries give designs and populations; the sources reviewed do not report results.

A review summarised in an encyclopedia source found no evidence of improved night vision from bilberries, based on low-quality clinical studies [2]. No registered trial listed here is designed to test cosmetic changes in eye brightness or whiteness.

Review articles describe berry anthocyanins as antioxidants and discuss possible roles in cardiovascular, neurological and ocular health, but these are largely laboratory and population-level findings [13]. A mouse study reported that anthocyanin-rich bilberry extract improved blood sugar and insulin sensitivity through AMPK activation [14]. Cell studies have reported apoptosis in cancer cells exposed to bilberry anthocyanins [15]. These findings do not establish effects in people.

timeline.event: The Oxford English Dictionary records the first English use of the word bilberry, in writing by John Dee, as reported by Grokipedia [1].
Linnaeus formally names Vaccinium myrtillus in Species Plantarum [1].
